0.title: The Prayers of the Kingdom
0.overview:
The Psalter is the Bible's own hymnbook and prayer book — 150 poems spanning a thousand years of Israel's life with God, from the wilderness generation to the post-exilic community, collected into five books that mirror the structure of the Torah. Here Israel does not merely receive instruction about God; she speaks to God, and in doing so models for all God's people what it means to bring every dimension of human experience — joy, terror, guilt, gratitude, vengeance, wonder, despair, praise — into the presence of the living LORD.

The Psalter's subtitle, The Prayers of the Kingdom, captures two dimensions that must be held together. These are prayers — honest, embodied, often raw cries from real people in real history. But they are also kingdom prayers: they arise from and point toward David's throne, and ultimately to the greater David who would fulfill everything Israel's king was meant to be. As Athanasius wrote in the fourth century, 'the Psalter has a unique place in the Bible: most of Scripture speaks to us, but the Psalter speaks for us.' And as Dietrich Bonhoeffer recognized in the twentieth, 'the Psalter is the prayer book of Jesus Christ' — he prayed these words, wept these tears, sang these praises, and every Christian who prays the Psalms prays them in him.

The Five Books and their movement: Book I (Psalms 1–41) is primarily Davidic and personal — the individual before God. Book II (Psalms 42–72) expands to the community and the nation. Book III (Psalms 73–89) is the darkest book, wrestling with the Exile and the apparent failure of the Davidic covenant. Book IV (Psalms 90–106) responds with a theology of the LORD's eternal kingship — he reigned before David, he reigns when David's throne lies in ruins. Book V (Psalms 107–150) moves toward the great doxological finale, culminating in the five Hallelujah psalms (146–150) that end the Psalter in pure praise. The movement from lament to praise, from Psalm 1's two ways to Psalm 150's universal hallelujah, is the theological arc of the whole collection.

Psalm types: The Psalter contains several identifiable genres, each with its own rhetorical shape and pastoral function. Lament psalms (individual: 3, 5–7, 13, 22, 25–28, 31, 35–36, 38–40, 42–43, 51–57, 61, 63–64, 69–71, 86, 88, 102, 109, 120, 130, 140–143; communal: 12, 44, 58, 60, 74, 77–80, 83, 85, 89, 90, 94, 123, 126, 137) follow a recognizable structure: address, complaint, confession of trust, petition, and vow of praise. They teach that honest speech to God — even anguished speech — is itself an act of faith. Praise psalms (descriptive praise: 8, 19, 29, 33, 65, 100, 103–104, 111, 113–114, 117, 135–136, 145–150; declarative/thanksgiving: 18, 30, 32, 34, 40, 66, 92, 107, 116, 118, 138) form the other pole of the Psalter's emotional range. Royal psalms (2, 18, 20–21, 45, 72, 89, 101, 110, 132, 144) celebrate the Davidic king and find their ultimate fulfillment in Christ. Wisdom psalms (1, 37, 49, 73, 112, 119, 127–128, 133) reflect on Torah, retribution, and the good life. Zion psalms (46, 48, 76, 84, 87, 122) celebrate the city of God. Enthronement psalms (47, 93, 96–99) proclaim the LORD as king over all nations.

Superscriptions: About two-thirds of the psalms carry superscriptions — headings that appear in the Hebrew text and are considered part of the inspired text by the majority of Reformed interpreters. These identify authors (David, Asaph, the Sons of Korah, Solomon, Ethan, Heman, Moses), provide musical and liturgical instructions (lamnatseach = 'to the choirmaster'; miktam, maskil, shir), and sometimes indicate historical settings (Psalms 3, 7, 18, 34, 51–52, 54, 56–57, 59–60, 63, 142). The Davidic attribution of 73 psalms is historically reliable and pastorally significant: these are not anonymous liturgical compositions but the prayers of a king who knew both the throne and the cave, the victory and the adultery, the covenant and the exile of his own sin.

Christ in the Psalms: The New Testament cites the Psalms more than any other OT book — over 70 direct citations and hundreds of allusions. The apostles understood the Psalter as fundamentally Christological. Key Messianic psalms include: Psalm 2 (the Son installed on Zion; cited at Jesus's baptism, transfiguration, and resurrection); Psalm 8 (Son of Man given dominion; cited in Hebrews 2); Psalm 16 (not abandoned to Sheol; cited in Acts 2 for the resurrection); Psalm 22 (forsakenness, crucifixion details, vindication; Jesus's cry from the cross); Psalm 40 (the body prepared, the scroll written; cited in Heb. 10); Psalm 45 (the king whose throne is forever; cited in Heb. 1); Psalm 69 (zeal for God's house; reproaches; betrayal); Psalm 72 (the universal king); Psalm 89 (the Davidic covenant); Psalm 110 (the Lord at the right hand, priest after Melchizedek — the most-cited psalm in the NT); Psalm 118 (the rejected stone made cornerstone). Reading the Psalms Christologically does not evacuate their historical meaning but fulfills it: Jesus is the true Israel, the true David, the true Son of God who prayed these prayers in his flesh, and in whom all the kingdom prayers find their Yes.

The Psalms of Ascent (120–134): This collection of 15 psalms was sung by pilgrims ascending to Jerusalem for the three annual festivals (Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles). Their brevity, their recurring imagery of Zion and the LORD's protection, and their movement from individual distress (Ps. 120) to communal worship (Ps. 134) made them ideal for the journey. Alec Motyer calls them 'the pilgrim's companion' — a microcosm of the whole Psalter's movement from where we are to where God dwells.

The Imprecatory Psalms: Several psalms contain curses against enemies (35, 58, 69, 83, 109, 137, 139) that disturb modern readers. C. S. Lewis in Reflections on the Psalms acknowledged the difficulty honestly — these are not pleasant. But Derek Kidner and John Piper offer the essential framework: (1) these are cries to God, not acts of personal revenge — the psalmist hands justice to God rather than taking it himself; (2) they arise from a world where wickedness was destroying the covenant community; (3) they are ultimately Christological — Jesus himself applies Psalm 69's curse ('Let his place be desolate') to Judas (Acts 1:20); and (4) they express a passion for God's justice that the comfortable church has largely lost. The Christian prays them in Christ, against the real enemies — sin, death, and the devil — whose defeat was accomplished at the cross.

Psalm 119: The great Torah psalm stands at the center of Book V and is the longest chapter in the Bible — 176 verses in 22 acrostic stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Every verse (with one possible exception) refers to the Word of God by one of eight synonyms: Torah, testimony, precepts, statutes, commandments, rules, word, promise. It is not legalistic duty but passionate longing: 'Oh how I love your law! It is my meditation all the day' (v. 97). VanGemeren calls it 'the alphabet of devotion.' Spurgeon devoted a separate volume of the Treasury of David to it alone.

The Hallel (113–118 and 146–150): The Egyptian Hallel (113–118) was sung at Passover — Psalms 113–114 before the meal, 115–118 after. Jesus and his disciples sang these at the Last Supper (Matt. 26:30). The Great Hallel (136) was also part of the Passover liturgy. The final Hallel (146–150) closes the entire Psalter with five consecutive psalms of pure praise, each opening and closing with Hallelujah — the Hebrew imperative 'Praise the LORD!' The Psalter ends not with a question or a lament but with a doxology that encompasses all creation. This is where all prayer is heading.

1.title: The Two Ways
1.text: Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, nor stands in the way of sinners, nor sits in the seat of scoffers; but his delight is in the law of the LORD, and on his law he meditates day and night. (ESV)
1.overview:
Psalm 1 is the gateway to the entire Psalter — not so much a psalm as a doorkeeper, standing at the entrance and asking every reader a single question: Which path are you on? Derek Kidner calls it 'a wisdom psalm that serves as a preface to the whole collection,' and Calvin opens his commentary on the Psalms by noting that this short poem contains the seed of everything that follows. The placement is deliberate: before Israel sings anything else, she must know that the shape of a blessed life is Torah-shaped.

The psalm divides the whole of human existence into two trajectories — the righteous and the wicked — with no middle ground and no possibility of neutrality. This binary is not harsh moralism but pastoral realism: there really are two ways, two destinations, two verdicts. The New Testament will echo this structure in the Sermon on the Mount's two builders, two gates, two trees. Jesus himself is the fulfillment of this psalm: the one Man who never walked in the counsel of the wicked, whose delight in the law was perfect, whose way the LORD knew and kept.

Structurally, the psalm moves from the beatitude of the righteous man (vv. 1–3) to the fate of the wicked (vv. 4–5) to the LORD's sovereign verdict that undergirds both (v. 6). Kidner notes the artful contrast: the righteous man is planted and permanent; the wicked are chaff — weightless, directionless, driven by any wind. The psalm is not about moral effort but about orientation: where does a life draw its nourishment?

sections.title: The Blessed Man: Walking, Standing, Sitting
sections.commentary:
The Hebrew ashre — 'blessed' — is a plural of intensity meaning 'O the happinesses of!' It is not a divine pronouncement from above but a wisdom exclamation: look at this man, look how alive he is! Spurgeon notes that the Psalter opens not with a command but a beatitude — grace before law, joy before duty. The same word opens the Sermon on the Mount (Matt. 5:3–11), and the echo is not accidental.

Verse 1 describes the blessed man by three refusals arranged in a descending spiral: walking in the counsel of the wicked, standing in the way of sinners, sitting in the seat of scoffers. Kidner observes that the progression from walking to standing to sitting pictures increasing immersion — what begins as casual association solidifies into identity. The 'scoffer' (letz) is the most hardened figure in wisdom literature: the man who has moved beyond doubt into contempt, who mocks what is holy and cannot be corrected (Prov. 9:7–8). The blessed man never takes that seat.

But the positive definition in v. 2 is the real heart of the portrait. His delight is in the Torah — not merely his obedience, but his joy. He meditates (hagah — the low sound of murmuring, like a lion growling over prey, Isa. 31:4) day and night. VanGemeren notes this is not academic study but rumination — the Word rolling through the mind until it shapes desire. Calvin: 'He who would profit in the school of God must meditate upon his law day and night… he alone is truly wise who has learned to do God's will.'

sections.title: The Tree by the Stream
sections.commentary:
'He is like a tree planted by streams of water.' The image is of deliberate transplanting — not a tree that happened to sprout near water, but one purposefully set there. Kidner: 'The point is permanence and productivity, not self-sufficiency.' The tree does not produce its own water; it is rooted where the water flows. So the righteous man does not generate his own life — he is rooted in the Word, and the Word is his supply.

The fruitfulness is seasonal ('its fruit in its season') — a note of realism. The blessed life is not one of unbroken prosperity but of yield at the right time. And the leaf does not wither: even in drought, the deep-rooted tree retains vitality. This is the picture Jeremiah draws in 17:7–8, almost verbatim — proof that both prophets are drawing on a shared wisdom tradition about the life hidden in God.

The closing line — 'In all that he does, he prospers' — must be read carefully. This is not a health-and-wealth promise but a covenantal orientation: the man whose root is in God will find that his life has direction, meaning, and ultimate fruit. Spurgeon: 'The ungodly have their best things first; the righteous have theirs last.' The prosperity of Psalm 1 is eschatological before it is material — it points forward to the day when the Two Ways reach their final destinations.

sections.title: Chaff: The Wicked Have No Weight
sections.commentary:
'Not so the wicked.' The abruptness of the Hebrew (lo ken ha-resha'im) is intentional — a slap of contrast. Everything said of the tree is reversed. The wicked are not planted, not fruitful, not permanent. They are chaff — the papery husks beaten off grain and tossed skyward, utterly at the mercy of the wind. Spurgeon called this 'the most terrible of all metaphors': no root, no weight, no substance. The image recurs in Isaiah 17:13, Daniel 2:35, and Hosea 13:3 — always signifying that which history will simply blow away.

Verse 5 draws the forensic conclusion: the wicked will not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous. The 'standing' here echoes v. 1's 'standing in the way of sinners' — the wicked chose not to stand with the righteous in this life; they will find they cannot stand with them in the judgment. Kidner: 'Their exclusion is their own achievement.' The 'congregation of the righteous' anticipates the final assembly of God's people — what Revelation calls the marriage supper of the Lamb.

For the preacher: do not soften the two-way structure. Tim Keller observes that our culture desperately wants a third option — spiritual but not religious, moral but not committed — and Psalm 1 will not provide one. Every neutral-seeming path eventually curves toward one of two destinations.

sections.title: The LORD Knows the Way
sections.commentary:
The psalm's final verse is its theological foundation: 'for the LORD knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish.' The two-way structure of the whole psalm rests not on human choice alone but on divine knowledge. The verb yada — 'to know' — carries in Hebrew the full weight of relational intimacy: the LORD does not merely observe the righteous man, he knows him, is present with him, guards him (cf. 2 Tim. 2:19, 'The Lord knows those who are his').

Spurgeon: 'The LORD's eye is always upon the path of the godly — not merely to observe but to approve, to direct, and to defend.' This is the ground of all the stability in vv. 1–3: the tree is planted securely not because the righteous man is virtuous but because the LORD's knowledge is his foundation. Calvin: 'Since God is our keeper, our condition, however hard it may be in the eyes of men, is in reality supremely happy.'

The perishing of the wicked way is the logical consequence of having no such divine knowing. It is not that God abandons the wicked — it is that a path chosen in rejection of God leads, by its own internal logic, to dissolution. The way will perish is a future of certainty: history moves toward the day when every path reaches its end. Christologically, Jesus is the one Righteous Man whose way the Father knew perfectly — and whose resurrection is the first-fruits of the righteous way reaching its full destination.

1.theology:
Theme. Psalm 1 is a wisdom psalm functioning as the theological preface to the Psalter. Its central claim is that human existence is structured by a fundamental binary: the way of the righteous (Torah-rooted, LORD-known, fruitful) and the way of the wicked (rootless, chaff-like, perishing). The psalm is not moralistic — it does not say 'try harder'; it says 'where are you rooted?' The blessed life flows from delight in God's Word, which is itself a gift of grace.

Christological connection. Jesus is the singular fulfillment of the blessed man of Psalm 1: the one who never walked in the counsel of the wicked, whose delight in Torah was perfect, whose way the Father knew perfectly. His resurrection is the ultimate vindication of the righteous way. The Christian reads this psalm Christologically first — and then, in Christ, finds it to be their own calling and destiny (Rom. 8:1).

Canonical function. As the Psalter's doorkeeper, Psalm 1 frames the entire collection as instruction for life (Torah) before it is worship. The Psalter will teach Israel to pray — but first it teaches her what kind of person can approach God: the one who is rooted in his Word.
1.examples:
Then: In post-exilic Israel, the returnees from Babylon faced a culture where the counsel of surrounding nations — compromise with idolatry, intermarriage, pragmatic accommodation — was seductive. Psalm 1's opening negative portrait was a call to a distinct, Torah-shaped identity in a pluralistic world. Ezra and Nehemiah read as living commentaries on this psalm.

Now: The contemporary equivalent of 'walking in the counsel of the wicked' is the ambient counsel of secular culture absorbed through media, entertainment, and professional formation — the slow drift toward a worldview where God is marginal and self is sovereign. The antidote is not counter-cultural rage but what v. 2 prescribes: a rival delight. The person who meditates on God's Word day and night is not suppressing desires — they are cultivating better ones. As Keller puts it: 'You don't fight delight with duty. You fight delight with greater delight.'
